title: Dolly Parton’s “Dollitics” and the Possibilities of Uniting
author: Daniel Warner
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/dpladysmithblack-680x511.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/09/04/dolly-
partons-dollitics-and-the-possibilities-of-uniting/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/dpladysmithblack-680x511.png)

Dolly Parton performs with Ladysmith Black Mambazo. (Screen capture from video
posted to [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gYq4gA7r49I).)

The death of Dolly Parton made front pages around the world. “Country music
star’s songs spoke to millions” was the _New York Times_ headline. The story
of the poor girl from Appalachia reaching fame, stardom and riches was the
archetypical American Dream come true. “We like Dolly Parton because we like
that story about who we are,” sociologist Tressie McMillan Cottom wrote. But
what really piqued my curiosity was the _Times_ line: “She was,
quintessentially, a uniter of people.”

Is it possible to be a “uniter of people” today? Parton seemed to have all
poles of U.S. politics on her side. From the left, the Democratic Socialist
mayor of New York Zohran Mamdani called her an “irreplaceable champion of the
working class.” On the right, the Republican Party of Tennessee, her home
state, [declared her](https://www.facebook.com/TNGOP/posts/remembering-dolly-
parton-a-gifted-musician-an-advocate-for-children-
everywhere-a/1613445007005616/) a “treasure,” while Greg Abbott, the
Republican governor of Texas,
[said](https://x.com/GregAbbott_TX/status/2092327533907710396) “God Bless
Dolly.” After her death, President Trump called her “one of the greatest
Country singers,” and said, “There has never been anyone like her, and never
will.” Trump ordered U.S. flags to be flown at half-staff nationwide through
September 1, 2026, in her honor—a notably rare tribute for an entertainer.

Parsing her politics is not difficult. “My daddy was a Republican, my mama was
a Democrat, and I’m a hypocrite!” [she once joked in a television
interview](https://x.com/RonFilipkowski/status/2092320669115548157). “Of
course, I have my opinion about everybody and everything,” she once [told an
interviewer](https://www.instagram.com/reels/DUaxtzhDgw7/), “but I learned a
long time ago, keep your damn mouth shut if you want to stay in show
business.”

One of her nephews, Bryan Seaver, who announced her death [on social
media](https://www.instagram.com/reels/DceNXgPJyZ9/), referred to her
particular brand of political neutrality as “Dollitics.”

Is it possible to be neutral today? A well-known pundit, Ron Brownstein,
described the different poles in current U.S. politics as the difference
between beer and wine drinkers: beer drinkers on the right, wine drinkers on
the left. Culturally, Dolly certainly was closer to the beer
drinkers—Tennessee, country music, Christianity, rural America; but her
popularity indicates Dollitics cut across beverage preferences.

As far as arguments over neutrality, the question is not confined to American
politics nor to being able to enjoy wine and beer. Soon, on September 27,
Swiss voters will be asked what their historic neutrality means as they decide
whether neutrality should be enshrined in the Swiss Constitution.

Parton’s Dollitics was not a formal, legal neutrality like Switzerland’s. It
was, at least in part, pragmatic. If she wanted to be successful, she had to
appeal to all listeners, left and right. Swiss neutrality also has elements of
self-interest; neutrality is a reasonable position for a small country
surrounded by three major European powers: France, Germany and Italy.

But beyond neutrality, and tied to Dollitics, is the question of being a
uniter. Parton stayed out of partisan politics. She refused offers of the
Presidential Medal of Freedom from both President Biden and President Trump.
But Dolly had opinions. She supported LGBTQ rights publicly and told one
interviewer, “And of course Black lives Matter.” She simply didn't make
partisan political identity her brand. Similarly, Swiss neutrality did not
stop Switzerland from joining European countries in sanctioning Russia after
its invasion of Ukraine.

Today, the Democratic Party is being torn by tensions between Democratic
Socialists and the traditional, established Party. Republicans are being
stretched by MAGA followers and traditional Republicans fearful that Trump and
MAGA will cause disastrous results in the midterm elections.

Both Democrats and Republicans are having problems keeping their voters within
expanding tents.

Given the polarizations within the two major political parties and between the
parties, is there a possibility of a uniter in America today? Parton was a
singer, songwriter, actress, and philanthropist; all outside the political
realm. The uniqueness of Trump’s calling for flags to be flown at half-mast
for an entertainer shows how special she was.

But is the notion of being a uniter also unique today? Identity politics
places people in a definitive box. Titles such as radical, progressive,
centrist and conservative leave little room for general comments about
humanity and the common good.

Dolly could speak to people without requiring them to agree with her, whereas
modern political identity seems to say: Before I listen to what you say, I
need to know which box you belong in.

Dolly may have been nonpartisan without being neutral. Switzerland may be
neutral without being apolitical. And a political “uniter” might not be
neutral at all—it might simply be someone who can hold strong views while
recognizing the legitimacy and humanity of people who disagree.

One of the first lessons in teaching young diplomats is the phrase “We agree
to disagree.” The first “agree” may seem superficial, but it is the necessary
foundation for all that follows. It means I recognize that you are entitled to
your view even when I think you are wrong.

There are two words often used in Switzerland I have always had difficulty
understanding. The first is neutrality. This boy from the Bronx too often
equates neutrality with pacifism. But Swiss neutrality has not always meant
sitting on the sidelines. Micheline Calmy-Rey, the former Swiss foreign
minister and president, calls it “active neutrality.” For example, after
Russia and Georgia broke diplomatic relations following their 2008 war,
Switzerland represented the interests of Georgia in Moscow and Russia in
Tbilisi. Neutrality, in that case, meant keeping open a channel between two
countries that no longer talked to each other.

Dolly could sing to both sides. Switzerland could mediate with both sides.
Neither required agreement, except to listen and to talk.

The second word is consensus. Is it possible today in the United States? Can
we agree to disagree and recognize each other as legitimate? Can we disagree
without making disagreement the reason to reject the other person?

Dolly Parton was a uniter, not a political partisan. Her example shows that a
uniter isn't just someone who stands in the middle abstaining from expressing
her opinion. It is someone who takes a position while refusing to make the
person on the other side illegitimate. Can there be a politician in the United
States today who is a uniter and can do that?
